title: Blowfish Hangover Review: Does Aspirin + Caffeine Actually Work?
excerpt: An honest Blowfish for Hangovers review: what's in it (aspirin and caffeine), what it helps and what it doesn't, aspirin-and-alcohol safety, cheaper alternatives, and how it compares with DHM.
metaDescription: Honest Blowfish hangover review: aspirin + caffeine ingredients, does it work, aspirin and alcohol safety, user sentiment, and cheaper alternatives.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest verdict first:** Blowfish for Hangovers does what its ingredients can do, and not much more. Each dose is 1,000 mg of aspirin plus 120 mg of caffeine in a fizzy, buffered tablet you dissolve in water. That combination is a well-studied way to relieve a headache and take the edge off fatigue, so plenty of people find it genuinely helps the morning after. But it is a pain reliever with a hangover label, not a hangover cure. It does little for nausea, it doesn't rehydrate you beyond the glass of water you mix it in, and [aspirin carries real stomach-bleeding risks when combined with alcohol](/never-hungover/aspirin-and-alcohol). You can get almost the same ingredients for less from generic products.

**Who it suits:** an otherwise healthy adult who occasionally wakes up with a pounding head and sluggishness after a night out, who has no stomach problems, isn't on blood thinners, and is fine with aspirin. **Who should skip it:** anyone with ulcers, reflux, bleeding problems, aspirin allergy or asthma triggered by aspirin, kidney disease, anyone on blood thinners or daily NSAIDs, anyone who is pregnant, and anyone under 18.

> **This is not medical advice.** Blowfish is an over-the-counter drug that contains aspirin, and aspirin interacts with alcohol and with many medicines. Read the full Drug Facts label and **talk to your doctor or pharmacist before using it** if you take any prescription medicine, have a stomach, bleeding, kidney, liver or heart condition, or drink three or more drinks most days. **Get medical help right away** if you notice black or tarry stools, vomit that looks like coffee grounds or contains blood, severe stomach pain, ringing in the ears, or signs of an allergic reaction. In an emergency, call 911.

## What Is Blowfish for Hangovers?

Blowfish for Hangovers is an effervescent tablet made by Rally Labs, a small US company. You drop two tablets into a glass of water, wait for them to fizz and dissolve, and drink the result. It has been sold since the early 2010s and is widely available in drugstores, convenience stores and online.

The big selling point in its marketing is that Blowfish is an FDA-regulated over-the-counter drug rather than a dietary supplement. That claim is fair, but it's worth understanding what it means. Blowfish follows the FDA's long-standing rules (called an OTC monograph) for aspirin and caffeine pain relievers. Those rules cover ingredients that the FDA already accepts as safe and effective at certain doses for things like headache, body aches and drowsiness. It does **not** mean the FDA tested Blowfish as a hangover treatment or concluded that it treats hangovers as a whole. It means the ingredients, doses and label meet the standard for a pain reliever and alertness aid.

That's actually a point in its favor compared with many hangover products. Supplements don't need FDA approval before they go on sale, and their doses and claims can be loosely policed. With Blowfish, you know exactly what you're getting, in a consistent dose, made under drug manufacturing rules.

## Blowfish Ingredients: What's Actually in It

The active ingredients per two-tablet dose are:

| Ingredient | Amount per dose (2 tablets) | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Aspirin | 1,000 mg (500 mg per tablet) | Pain reliever and anti-inflammatory (an NSAID) |
| Caffeine | 120 mg (60 mg per tablet) | Stimulant that reduces drowsiness and boosts pain relief |

The inactive ingredients include the usual effervescent base, such as citric acid and sodium bicarbonate (baking soda), which create the fizz and buffer the aspirin, plus flavoring. Check the current package for the full list, since inactive ingredients can change.

For perspective:

- **1,000 mg of aspirin** is a full adult dose, the same as three regular 325 mg aspirin tablets, or two "extra strength" 500 mg tablets.
- **120 mg of caffeine** is roughly what you'd get from a large cup of brewed coffee. An 8-ounce cup of brewed coffee typically has somewhere around 80 to 100 mg, though it varies a lot.

So there are no secret ingredients, no vitamins, no herbal blends and no electrolytes in meaningful amounts. That simplicity is both the product's strength and its limit.

## Does Blowfish Hangover Actually Work?

This is the question most people searching for Blowfish want answered, so here it is plainly: **Blowfish works on some hangover symptoms, specifically headache, body aches and grogginess. There is no good evidence that it treats a hangover as a whole.**

### What the ingredients are good at

**Aspirin is a proven headache reliever.** Aspirin has decades of clinical trial data behind it for tension-type headaches and migraines. It works by blocking enzymes (called COX enzymes) that make prostaglandins, chemical messengers involved in pain and inflammation. Hangover headaches aren't exactly the same as tension headaches or migraines, but there's reason to think inflammation plays a part. Research has found that the immune system's signaling molecules (cytokines) are elevated during a hangover, and that their levels track with how bad people feel. An anti-inflammatory painkiller is a sensible tool against that.

There is also a small amount of older hangover-specific evidence for this drug class. A small trial published in the journal *Cephalalgia* in the early 1980s found that tolfenamic acid, a prescription NSAID in the same broad family as aspirin, reduced several hangover symptoms when taken around drinking compared with placebo. That's a single, old study of a different drug, so it's only weak support, but it points in the same direction as the anti-inflammatory theory.

**Caffeine makes painkillers work a bit better.** A Cochrane review on caffeine as an add-on to common painkillers (Derry and colleagues, updated in 2014) found that adding around 100 mg or more of caffeine to a standard dose of a painkiller like aspirin or acetaminophen gave a small but real increase in the number of people who got good pain relief. That's why so many headache products, from Excedrin to generic "headache formula" tablets, pair the two.

**Caffeine also fights the fog.** Part of a hangover is simply being tired, partly because alcohol wrecks sleep quality in the second half of the night. Caffeine reduces sleepiness and improves alertness. If you're a regular coffee drinker, it also heads off the caffeine-withdrawal headache you'd get from skipping your usual cup, which can quietly make a hangover morning worse.

### What it doesn't do

A hangover is not just a headache. It typically includes nausea, an upset stomach, fatigue, poor concentration, anxiety, sensitivity to light and sound, thirst and a general sense of feeling unwell. Scientists still don't fully understand all the causes, but the leading contributors include the immune response, disrupted sleep, a by-product of alcohol called acetaldehyde, irritation of the stomach lining, low blood sugar in some people, and mild dehydration.

Blowfish targets the pain and the sleepiness. It does nothing meaningful for:

- **Nausea and stomach upset.** Aspirin can actually irritate a stomach that alcohol has already inflamed. The buffering helps a little, but it doesn't make aspirin stomach-friendly.
- **Dehydration and electrolytes.** You drink the tablets in a glass of water, and that water helps. But the tablets themselves aren't an electrolyte drink.
- **Sleep loss and the deeper fatigue.** Caffeine masks tiredness for a few hours; it doesn't repay the sleep debt.
- **Anxiety and the shaky feeling.** Caffeine can make these worse in some people.

The broader research picture backs this up. Systematic reviews of hangover treatments, including one in the *BMJ* by Pittler, Verster and Ernst in 2005 and a later review published in *Addiction* in 2022, have found no compelling evidence that any remedy reliably prevents or treats hangovers as a whole. Most trials are small and of low quality. Blowfish's individual ingredients have strong evidence for pain relief; the product as a "hangover fix" does not have a body of hangover trials behind it.

### The fair conclusion

If your hangovers are mostly a headache and grogginess, Blowfish will likely help you feel noticeably better within an hour or so. If your hangovers are mostly nausea, misery and exhaustion, it will probably disappoint you. Our guide to [fast relief for hangover headaches](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025) covers other options for the pain, and our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) covers the stomach side, which Blowfish doesn't address.

## Is Blowfish Safe to Take After Drinking?

This deserves more attention than most reviews give it. Aspirin and alcohol are a combination that the FDA specifically warns about.

### The stomach-bleeding risk

Alcohol irritates the lining of the stomach. Aspirin does too, and it also reduces the stomach's natural protective mucus and makes platelets less sticky, so small injuries bleed more easily. Put together, the two raise the risk of stomach irritation, ulcers and gastrointestinal bleeding. That's why US labels on aspirin and other NSAIDs carry a stomach-bleeding warning, which specifically calls out people who **have three or more alcoholic drinks every day** while using the product.

For a healthy person who drinks occasionally, taking one labeled dose the morning after is a fairly common practice, and serious bleeding from a single dose is uncommon. But the risk is not zero, and it climbs with:

- Drinking heavily on a regular basis
- Taking aspirin repeatedly over several days
- Combining it with other NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) or blood thinners
- Being older, or having a history of ulcers or stomach bleeding
- Taking it on an empty stomach while the stomach lining is already irritated

### Never take it before or during drinking

The Blowfish label is aimed at the morning after, and that's the right time. Taking aspirin before or while drinking piles stomach irritation on top of stomach irritation. Some older research has also suggested that aspirin taken before drinking may modestly raise blood alcohol levels by slowing how much alcohol the stomach breaks down before it's absorbed. The effect seems small and the studies are dated, but it's one more reason not to take aspirin "pre-emptively."

### Who should not take Blowfish

Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before taking Blowfish, or skip it entirely, if you:

- Take **blood thinners** (such as warfarin, apixaban or clopidogrel) or a daily low-dose aspirin prescribed by a doctor
- Take other **NSAIDs**, steroids, or certain antidepressants (SSRIs and SNRIs can also raise bleeding risk)
- Have a history of **stomach ulcers, bleeding, reflux or gastritis**
- Have **asthma** that gets worse with aspirin or NSAIDs, or have had an allergic reaction to them
- Have **kidney disease, liver disease, high blood pressure or heart disease**
- Are **pregnant or breastfeeding**
- Are on a **sodium-restricted diet** (effervescent tablets usually contain a fair amount of sodium from the baking soda; check the label)
- Are sensitive to caffeine, have anxiety or heart rhythm problems, or are already having a lot of coffee
- Are **under 18**, because aspirin in children and teens is linked to a rare but serious condition called Reye's syndrome

For a deeper look at how pain relievers in the same family interact with alcohol, see our guide to [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol). The core message carries over: the risk mostly lands on the stomach and kidneys, and it rises with heavy drinking and repeated doses.

### When a hangover isn't just a hangover

If you vomit repeatedly and can't keep water down, if you're confused or very hard to wake, if you have chest pain, a severe headache unlike your usual ones, or a fever, don't treat it with Blowfish. Get medical help. Severe symptoms after drinking can signal alcohol poisoning or another problem that needs proper care. And if you ever see blood or "coffee grounds" in vomit, or black, tarry stools after taking aspirin, that's a sign of stomach bleeding and needs urgent attention.

## How to Take Blowfish (If You Do)

Follow the directions on the package you buy, as they're the legal label for that product. In general terms:

1. **Take it the morning after, not the night before.** Wait until you're actually awake and dealing with symptoms.
2. **Dissolve two tablets fully in a full glass of water.** Drinking the full glass is part of the benefit.
3. **Eat something if you can.** Even toast or crackers helps protect your stomach.
4. **Don't double up.** Don't take Blowfish alongside other aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen or combination headache pills. Check labels for "aspirin," "acetylsalicylic acid" or "salicylate."
5. **Count your caffeine.** If you also have two large coffees, you could easily be over 400 mg of caffeine for the morning, which is about where many people start to feel jittery and anxious.
6. **Keep drinking water and get some rest.** The tablets won't do that part for you.

## Blowfish vs Generic Alternatives

Here's the part that most Blowfish fans eventually discover: you can get very similar ingredients for less.

| Option | What's in it | How it compares |
|---|---|---|
| **Blowfish for Hangovers** | 1,000 mg aspirin + 120 mg caffeine per dose, effervescent | Convenient, consistent, pleasant to drink, but you pay a brand premium |
| **Alka-Seltzer Morning Relief** (and similar) | Aspirin + caffeine in an effervescent tablet | Very similar concept from a mainstream brand; check the label for exact doses |
| **Classic Alka-Seltzer** | Aspirin + a large dose of sodium bicarbonate, no caffeine | More antacid, no caffeine boost |
| **Plain aspirin + a cup of coffee** | 975 to 1,000 mg aspirin (tablets) + your own caffeine | Cheapest by far, nearly the same active ingredients, just not fizzy or buffered |
| **Ibuprofen or naproxen** | A different NSAID | Similar stomach caution with alcohol; some people find them better for aches |

Prices vary by store and pack size, so we won't quote figures that will go out of date. But per dose, Blowfish is usually noticeably more expensive than a store-brand aspirin and the coffee you'd drink anyway. What you're paying for is convenience, a dissolved format that some people find easier on a queasy stomach and quicker to kick in, and the fact that it's one packet you can keep in a bag or desk drawer.

That's a perfectly reasonable thing to pay for. Just know that the "hangover" branding isn't adding a different mechanism. It's the same aspirin and caffeine you can buy elsewhere.

### A note on Tylenol-based alternatives

Some people reach for acetaminophen (Tylenol) instead. It's gentler on the stomach but harder on the liver, and the alcohol combination has its own serious risks, especially for regular heavy drinkers. Products like Excedrin combine acetaminophen with aspirin and caffeine, which means you'd be taking on both sets of cautions. If you're choosing between painkillers after drinking, our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains the liver side in detail.

## What Real Users Say: Reddit and Review Sentiment

Looking across Reddit threads and retail reviews, a fairly consistent picture comes through. We're summarizing general patterns here rather than quoting individuals.

**What people like:**

- It works noticeably well for the **headache**, often within 20 to 45 minutes. That's the most common positive comment.
- The **caffeine kick** helps people get moving on a work morning.
- The **fizzy, dissolved format** goes down easier than swallowing pills when you feel rough, and the taste is generally described as tolerable to pleasant.
- It's **easy to carry**, in individually wrapped packets.

**What people complain about:**

- **It doesn't touch nausea** or the overall "poisoned" feeling. Many users say they still felt hungover, just with less of a headache.
- **Price.** A frequent comment is some version of "this is just aspirin and caffeine," followed by a switch to a cheaper generic.
- **Stomach discomfort** for some people, especially on an empty stomach.
- **Jitters or a racing heart** for people sensitive to caffeine or already shaky from the night before.
- **Expectations.** People who bought it expecting a cure tend to leave the harshest reviews. People who expected a good headache remedy tend to be satisfied.

That last point is the most useful takeaway. Satisfaction with Blowfish seems to depend almost entirely on whether you expected a painkiller or a miracle.

## Pros and Cons Summary

**Pros**

- Known ingredients with strong evidence for headache and pain relief
- Caffeine adds a modest boost to pain relief and helps with grogginess
- Regulated as an OTC drug, so the dose and quality are consistent
- Dissolved format is fast and easy on a rough morning
- Simple, honest formula with no hyped proprietary blends

**Cons**

- Treats symptoms, not the hangover itself; little help for nausea or fatigue
- Aspirin plus alcohol raises the risk of stomach irritation and bleeding
- Not suitable for many people (blood thinners, ulcers, asthma, pregnancy, under 18, kidney problems)
- Costs more than the generic equivalent
- Caffeine can worsen anxiety and jitters for some people
- Marketing language around "FDA" can make it sound more hangover-specific than it is

## Blowfish vs DHM: Different Tools for Different Jobs

People who search for Blowfish often compare it with DHM (dihydromyricetin), the plant compound this site focuses on. They aren't really competitors, because they do different jobs at different times.

| | Blowfish | DHM supplements |
|---|---|---|
| **When you take it** | The morning after | Usually around drinking (before or during), per most product directions |
| **What it targets** | Headache, aches and grogginess | Proposed effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver |
| **Regulatory status** | OTC drug | Dietary supplement |
| **Strength of evidence** | Strong for pain relief; no hangover-specific trials of the product | Promising early research, mostly in animals and the lab, with limited human data |
| **Main safety concern** | Stomach bleeding with alcohol; aspirin interactions | Generally well tolerated in available research; check interactions if on medication |

Blowfish is a reactive approach: you feel bad, you treat the pain. DHM is a proactive idea: it's taken around drinking in the hope of reducing how bad you feel later. The honest truth about DHM is that the research is encouraging but early. Our [honest review of the DHM science](/never-hungover/does-dhm-work-honest-science-review-2025) walks through what's known and what isn't, without the marketing.

You shouldn't think of either one as permission to drink more. The single most effective way to have a better morning is still to drink less, pace yourself with water, eat beforehand and protect your sleep. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) lays out the habits with the best evidence.

If you want to try DHM as part of that routine, two of the brands we rate are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people typically take and when. If you're on any medication, check with a pharmacist first, and don't combine a supplement plan with extra aspirin you don't need.

## The Bottom Line

- **Blowfish is aspirin (1,000 mg) plus caffeine (120 mg) in a fizzy tablet.** Nothing more mysterious than that.
- **It works well for hangover headaches and grogginess**, because those ingredients have strong evidence for pain and alertness.
- **There is no good evidence that it treats a hangover as a whole.** It won't fix nausea, sleep loss or the general misery.
- **Aspirin and alcohol together raise stomach-bleeding risk.** Take it only the morning after, with water and ideally food, never before or during drinking, and never on top of other NSAIDs.
- **Many people shouldn't take it at all**, including anyone on blood thinners or with ulcers, aspirin-sensitive asthma, kidney disease, pregnancy, or anyone under 18. Ask your doctor or pharmacist if you're unsure.
- **Generic aspirin and a cup of coffee get you most of the way there for less money.** Blowfish's real value is convenience.

Our verdict: a decent, honestly formulated headache remedy with a clever name, as long as you're a good candidate for aspirin and you go in expecting pain relief rather than a cure.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does Blowfish hangover actually work?**

It works on part of a hangover. Each dose has 1,000 mg of aspirin and 120 mg of caffeine, a combination with strong evidence for relieving headaches and reducing drowsiness, so many people feel noticeably better within an hour. There is no good evidence that it treats a hangover as a whole, though. It does little for nausea, an upset stomach, sleep loss or the general feeling of being unwell.

**What are the ingredients in Blowfish for Hangovers?**

The active ingredients are aspirin (500 mg per tablet) and caffeine (60 mg per tablet). The standard dose is two tablets dissolved in water, giving 1,000 mg of aspirin and 120 mg of caffeine. The inactive ingredients include an effervescent base such as citric acid and sodium bicarbonate, plus flavoring. Check the package for the current full list.

**Is Blowfish FDA approved?**

Blowfish is sold as an over-the-counter drug that follows the FDA's rules (the OTC monograph) for aspirin and caffeine pain relievers. That means its ingredients, doses and labeling meet an established federal standard, which is more oversight than most hangover supplements get. It does not mean the FDA tested it as a cure for hangovers. It's regulated as a pain reliever and alertness aid.

**Is it safe to take Blowfish after drinking alcohol?**

For a healthy adult who drinks occasionally, one labeled dose the morning after is a common practice, but it isn't risk-free. Aspirin and alcohol both irritate the stomach, and together they raise the risk of stomach irritation and bleeding. Take it with a full glass of water and ideally food, don't combine it with other NSAIDs, and don't take it before or during drinking. If you drink three or more drinks most days, take blood thinners, or have stomach, kidney or bleeding problems, talk to your doctor or pharmacist first.

**Can I take Blowfish before drinking to prevent a hangover?**

No. Blowfish is meant for the morning after. Taking aspirin before or while drinking adds stomach irritation on top of alcohol's, and some older research suggests aspirin taken beforehand may modestly raise blood alcohol levels. Wait until you wake up and actually have symptoms.

**Is Blowfish better than Alka-Seltzer or plain aspirin?**

Not in terms of what it does. Blowfish is very similar to other aspirin-and-caffeine effervescent tablets, and plain aspirin with a cup of coffee delivers nearly the same active ingredients for less money. What you pay extra for with Blowfish is convenience and a dissolved format that some people find easier on a rough morning. Classic Alka-Seltzer has more antacid but no caffeine.

**How much caffeine is in Blowfish?**

A standard two-tablet dose contains 120 mg of caffeine, which is roughly what you'd get from a large cup of brewed coffee. If you also drink coffee that morning, count it toward your total. Many people start to feel jittery or anxious above about 400 mg in a day, and caffeine can make the shaky, anxious side of a hangover worse.

**Who should not take Blowfish?**

Skip it, or ask a doctor or pharmacist first, if you take blood thinners or other NSAIDs, have a history of ulcers or stomach bleeding, have asthma triggered by aspirin, have kidney, liver or heart disease, are pregnant or breastfeeding, are on a low-sodium diet, or are sensitive to caffeine. It's not for anyone under 18 because of the link between aspirin and Reye's syndrome in young people.

**Is Blowfish the same as DHM?**

No. Blowfish is an aspirin and caffeine pain reliever taken the morning after to treat symptoms. DHM is a plant-based dietary supplement usually taken around drinking, with early research on how it may affect alcohol metabolism and the liver. They work in different ways and at different times, and neither one makes heavy drinking safe.
